messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mr. Kumar, a 61-year-old South Asian paramedic who has been married for over three decades, experienced a traumatic incident that profoundly altered his life several months ago. During a call involving an industrial accident, he was exposed to a toxic chemical leak that left him gasping for air and in immense pain. The moment the noxious fumes filled the space around him, Mr. Kumar felt as if he were drowning in darkness. He remembers frantically trying to escape, only to be overwhelmed by the overpowering smell of alcohol-like chemicals, which triggered a terrifying sensation that the environment was closing in on him. Since then, the event has become an enduring presence in his life. The mere sight or smell of anything reminiscent of that day can instantly transport him back to the horror he experienced. On one particularly dark night while working, Mr. Kumar found himself standing at the edge of a building, surrounded by shadows and the faint scent of something chemical. Suddenly, the memory hit him like a tidal wave of terror, making it impossible for him to breathe or focus on his duties. He felt as if he were reliving that moment of sheer panic. In an attempt to cope with these overwhelming memories, Mr. Kumar has adopted several maladaptive strategies. He spends most of his time ruminating about how the incident could have been prevented—had they taken different precautions or followed a different protocol. This rumination often leaves him feeling trapped in a cycle of "what if" scenarios that do little to alleviate his anxiety. To avoid being alone with these thoughts, Mr. Kumar keeps himself constantly surrounded by people. He frequents social gatherings and has even made it a point to be the life of every party he attends. Despite the superficial joy this constant socializing might bring, deep down, he is acutely aware that it is merely a façade designed to keep his fears at bay. Mr. Kumar’s avoidance behaviors have also extended to medical cues. Hospitals and ambulances, once symbols of help and safety in his line of work, now trigger intense anxiety. The mere thought of being examined or even stepping into an ambulance makes him feel as though he is about to relive the terror of that dark day. The consequences of these avoidance behaviors have been significant. His work performance has suffered, and he often finds himself unable to complete tasks that once came naturally to him. This decline in professional capability has strained his relationships with colleagues and superiors, who struggle to understand why the once reliable Mr. Kumar now seems so hesitant and distant. Moreover, his constant socializing has started to take a toll on his marriage. His wife has noticed a marked change in his behavior—she finds it difficult to get him alone for meaningful conversations or intimate moments. Instead of sharing his fears and anxieties with her, he has become more isolated, pushing others away even as he tries to surround himself with them. What finally brought Mr. Kumar to seek help was the realization that these coping mechanisms were no longer working. The memories continued to overwhelm him without warning, often leaving him feeling paralyzed in both his personal and professional life. He is most afraid of losing control entirely—of never being able to return to a state where he feels safe and capable. Despite his fears, Mr. Kumar holds onto hope that with the right support, he can reclaim some semblance of normalcy. He hopes for a future where the memories no longer consume him, where he can once again work without dread and connect with those around him in meaningful ways. The journey to healing is daunting, but he sees it as his only chance at regaining control over his life.
